messages:
Rachel: Heads up — saw a p99 tail latency jump to ~28s in us-west at ~12:16 UTC. pool-3 GPU util ~98% and queue_depth spiked. Looks like a large batch ingestion hit and flooded the single FIFO queue we use for that pool. Should we rethink FIFO-across-routes? Per-route queues or priority queues? :thinking:
Dan: +1. FIFO across the whole pool is noisy-neighbor heaven. My quick take: per-route queues for isolation, but keep a pool-level admission controller that enforces capacity and emits 429/Retry-After for low-priority routes when saturated. That gives predictable SLOs for interactive routes.
Sophie: Per-route seems sensible but watch out for route-level denial via parallelism. We need per-route concurrency caps + an expected-cost token (credit) so a route that spawns many long-token calls doesn't starve others. Also include token accounting by expected output tokens, not just requests.
Evan: We ran sims on priority queues + aging last Q. Findings: static priority led to starvation of medium-priority routes if a few high-prio long-running jobs started. Hybrid idea: per-route queues, prioritized classes (interactive, batch, background) + priority decay (age factor) so long-waiters rise in priority. Works well in sims.
Rachel: That hybrid matches my intuition. Operational questions: how many priority classes? Do we allow routes to opt-in as 'burstable' with a cost budget? And what should autoscaler do — scale pool vs spill to another region vs reject?
Dan: For classes, keep it simple: interactive (p99 SLO), standard, batch. Allow burstable flag with per-customer monthly budget and short-term burst tokens. Autoscaler: prefer scale-up in-region if capacity cheap, otherwise spill to another region with multi-region routing + fallback. Reject only when cross-region latency or cost would violate SLO/cost budget.
Sophie: Also need observability hooks: per-route queue depth, per-class wait time, admission rejects, and a fairness metric (median wait per-customer). Add alert when median(wait|interactive)>100ms or pool_util>0.95 for >2m.
ops-bot: [automated] pool-3: 2026-03-10T12:16Z pool3_queue_depth=87 pool3_util=0.98 p99=28.2s triggered alert rule infra.pool.high_util. link: https://console.redwood.ai/dash/pools/pool-3/alerts/3421
Evan: Example config sketch (talking config, not literal API):

```yaml
pool_policy:
  queueing: per-route
  classes: [interactive, standard, batch]
  admission:
    type: token_bucket
    pool_capacity_tokens: 100000
    route_cost: tokens_per_expected_output_token
  priority_decay: 
    enabled: true
    half_life_s: 60
  concurrency_caps:
    default: 8
    route_overrides: {}
```

Rachel: Nice. A few follow-ups: 1) what are the token accounting numbers we should use for Llama-like vs transformer-large quantized models? 2) edge case: if many interactive requests are short but arrive in bursts, we need short-term burst capacity else we throttle user UX.
Dan: For token accounting, start with tokens_per_token = 1 for baseline and calibrate by model profile (quantization yields ~0.6 cost). We'll get profiling numbers from runtime team. Bursting: give interactive a small burst budget (e.g., 10 concurrent tokens) per route, replenished slowly.
Sophie: Operational playbook addition: when pool_util>0.9 and queueing rejects > 1% for >5m, run immediate mitigation: 1) enable emergency-burst for interactive for 1m, 2) kick an autoscale request, 3) set alert for oncall to investigate noisy routes.
Rachel: Sounds actionable. I'll draft a runbook + config proposal and tag runtime/ops for numbers. @Dan @Evan @Sophie — can you review the YAML next 24h?
Dan: Will review.
Evan: On it, will attach sim results and numbers.
Sophie: Reviewing tomorrow AM.
